topics.title: Requirement and deliberate boundaries
topics.summary: HarborRoutes reads a small directed weighted graph and one source/target query. It either prints one minimum-cost route or reports that the target is unreachable. The application combines bounded parsing, adjacency lists, a priority queue, shortest-path reasoning, predecessor reconstruction, independent witnesses, and deterministic command-line fixtures. It runs locally and performs no network communication.

blocks.text: The input is an ASCII whitespace-separated token stream. The first four fields are vertex count, edge count, source, and target. Each following edge contributes three fields: from, to, and nonnegative weight. Vertex count is between one and 128, edge count is at most 4,096, and weights are at most 1,000,000. Vertex identifiers are dense zero-based indices. Exactly the declared fields must be present, with no trailing token.

blocks.text: Tokens contain unsigned decimal digits only, with at most twelve characters. Leading zeros are allowed within that length. Signs, decimal points, non-ASCII numerals, and oversized fields are rejected. The parser bounds a token before appending another character. It does not first read an arbitrarily large line and only afterward check its size.

blocks.text: These limits bound retained graph and token storage for accepted inputs. topics.title: Select the algorithm from the weight contract
topics.summary: Dijkstra’s method is appropriate here because every edge weight is nonnegative. The priority queue chooses the smallest currently known tentative distance. Once that entry is current rather than stale, no path through a later nonnegative extension can improve a finalized smaller distance. This argument would fail with unrestricted negative edges, so rejecting them is part of the algorithm selection, not merely a parser preference.

blocks.text: The implementation uses immutable (distance, vertex) queue entries instead of trying to mutate heap priorities in place. An improved distance pushes a new entry. When an older entry reaches the top, it is discarded if its stored distance differs from the current best distance for that vertex. The target can be returned early only after this stale-entry check.

blocks.text: Adjacency lists are sorted after parsing. Queue pairs also use the vertex identifier as a tie-breaker, and predecessor updates occur only on strict improvement. These choices provide deterministic results for reordered edge records in the tested contract. They do not promise the lexicographically smallest path among all equal-cost paths. Zero-weight edges are allowed; avoiding equal-cost predecessor rewrites also prevents casual creation of cycles in the predecessor chain.

blocks.text: The graph is validated again at the public algorithm boundary so programmatically constructed requests cannot bypass size, endpoint, and weight checks. The parser and solver therefore have related but independent responsibilities. Internal arithmetic includes an explicit overflow guard even though the accepted graph bounds keep a simple shortest path far below the maximum uint64_t value.

topics.title: Define ownership and the commit point
topics.summary: Request owns its adjacency lists. Route owns its vertex sequence. Neither exposes a borrowed view whose lifetime depends on a local parsing buffer. The load function parses into a candidate request, then moves that completed candidate into the accepted state. A compile-time check verifies that this particular move assignment is nonthrowing.

blocks.text: If parsing or allocation fails before the commit, the previous accepted request remains unchanged. This guarantee concerns the in-memory request. It does not rewind the input stream or remove already consumed bytes. Similarly, detecting a failed output stream does not erase the prefix already written to an external destination. The regression tests demonstrate these limits explicitly.

topics.title: Command-line boundary
topics.summary: The process returns zero for both a route and an unreachable result. Input errors return two; other caught standard exceptions return three. A successful output call is followed by a flush and another stream-state check. This detects reported local output failure, not whether a downstream person or remote storage system has durably received the result.

topics.title: Validate a path independently of the priority queue
topics.summary: The test oracle uses an all-pairs dynamic-programming calculation on tiny graphs. It initializes each diagonal to zero, keeps the minimum weight for parallel direct edges, and considers each vertex as an allowed intermediate. Comparing all source/target pairs on generated graphs checks more than one preferred route from one source.

blocks.text: Failure-injection tests interrupt input at every position in one bounded valid request, including the attempted read after its last byte. Each interruption must raise an input error and preserve the previously accepted request. A separate stream with exception masks enabled tests ordinary end-of-input handling. An output buffer accepts only a short prefix, then reports failure; the test confirms both the exception and the retained prefix.
